lessons.title: Why the AI Act exists
lessons.subtitle: 27 countries going it alone, one lesson from the GDPR, the CE tradition. That is how a single-market problem became the world's first AI law.

sections.title: 27 national AI laws in the pipeline
sections.content:
France had the CNIL. Spain built the AESIA. Italy's Garante banned ChatGPT in March 2023. By that year several Member States were drafting AI rules of their own, and without harmonisation a German SME would soon have been serving 27 compliance regimes in parallel, each with its own definitions, reporting duties, and fines.

Recital 3 of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 names the problem. Divergent national rules can fragment the internal market. In its guidelines the European Commission sets out two objectives: trustworthy AI in the internal market, and innovation alongside it (Article 1(1), points (a) and (h)).

**Legal basis:** Article 114 TFEU, the internal market. Not Article 16 TFEU, data protection. The AI Act treats AI as a product, not as a data problem. Everything else follows from that. Conformity assessment, technical documentation, market surveillance, CE marking.

**For you:** one set of rules, whether you deliver to Munich, Milan, or Madrid (Article 1(1)).
sections.keyTakeaway: One set of rules is cheaper for an SME than 27. The AI Act follows internal-market law (Article 114 TFEU), not data-protection law.

sections.title: Why voluntary commitments were not enough
sections.content:
Between 2019 and 2023 the voluntary guidance piled up. The OECD AI Principles, the Ethics Guidelines of the EU High-Level Expert Group, industry codes of every description. None of it stopped a large technology company from rolling out a problematic system. Social-scoring prototypes, mass biometric surveillance in public spaces, emotion recognition at work: all of it sat in a grey area.

Recital 8 draws the consequence. Harmonised rules are needed because voluntary codes do not protect fundamental rights well enough. The EU had learned from the GDPR that behaviour changes when the law binds, and not before.

**Brussels Effect 2.0:** whoever sells in the EU meets EU rules. And because nobody builds two product versions for 500 million consumers, the EU standard becomes the world standard. The GDPR showed how it works, and California's CCPA, Brazil's LGPD, and Japan's APPI followed. If OpenAI or Anthropic make their systems EU-compliant, every customer benefits from that groundwork. It does not replace your own deployer obligations (Recital 1).
sections.keyTakeaway: Voluntary codes did not protect fundamental rights, so Recital 8 calls for binding, harmonised rules. The Brussels Effect turns EU rules into world standards.

sections.title: The CE tradition, the Machinery Regulation, and product liability
sections.content:
The AI Act is not new territory. It is product-safety law. Through Regulation 765/2008, the New Legislative Framework, it hangs on the CE logic that every German machinery builder has known for decades. Conformity assessment, notified body, technical documentation, EU declaration of conformity, CE marking, market surveillance.

Anyone producing to CE rules today, whether for machinery, medical devices, or toys, already knows the mechanics. The AI Act lays one more layer on top. For many SMEs the AI part becomes another chapter in technical documentation that exists anyway.

**The GDPR still applies alongside:** Article 2(7) states that the Regulation is without prejudice to the General Data Protection Regulation. Whoever feeds personal data into an AI system complies with both. Duplicate work? No. Complementary duties: the GDPR governs whether you may process, the AI Act governs how the system has to work (Recital 9).

**A regulation, not a directive.** The AI Act is an EU regulation (Article 288(2) TFEU) and applies directly in all 27 Member States, with no national transposing statute. The prohibitions in Article 5 and the AI-literacy duty in Article 4 have applied directly since 2 February 2025. Germany does not need a law of its own before these duties reach you.
sections.keyTakeaway: The AI Act is product-safety law on the CE pattern. The GDPR and the AI Act apply side by side, and neither replaces the other.

quiz.questionText: What is the primary legal basis for the AI Act?

answerOptions.text: Article 114 TFEU, which concerns harmonisation of the internal market
Article 16 TFEU, which concerns data protection
Article 4 TEU, which concerns national security
Article 101 TFEU, which concerns competition law

quiz.explanation: The AI Act is an internal-market measure based on Article 114 TFEU. Recital 3 of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 explains its objective as preventing national fragmentation, not regulating data protection.

quiz.questionText: Why did the EU decide against relying only on voluntary commitments?

answerOptions.text: Voluntary codes had not been sufficient to protect fundamental rights
Because the GDPR already covers every AI risk
Because the OECD AI Principles apply only in the United States
Because voluntary commitments are unlawful in the EU

quiz.explanation: Recital 8 calls for harmonised rules because voluntary codes do not secure a high enough level of protection for fundamental rights. The GDPR had already shown it: behaviour changes when the law binds.

quiz.questionText: Which existing regulation does the AI Act supplement rather than replace?

answerOptions.text: The GDPR (Regulation (EU) 2016/679)
The Machinery Directive is replaced in full
CE marking no longer applies to AI products
The Product Liability Directive is repealed

quiz.explanation: Article 2(7) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 states that the AI Act is without prejudice to the GDPR. Recital 9 also places the AI Act within the EU's New Legislative Framework for product safety.

lessons.title: Roles: provider, deployer, importer, and distributor
lessons.subtitle: Your role decides most of your obligations. Many SMEs put themselves in the wrong one.

sections.title: Four roles, one regulation
sections.content:
Which role are you in? Article 3 of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 knows four, each with a word-precise legal definition, and the answer decides how far your obligations reach:

- **Provider (Article 3(3)):** develops an AI system and places it on the market under its own name or trademark. OpenAI, Microsoft, Aleph Alpha, SAP.
- **Deployer (Article 3(4)):** uses an AI system under its own authority in the course of a professional activity. Every SME with ChatGPT Enterprise, Personio, or an AI feature in DATEV.
- **Authorised representative (Article 3(5)):** a person established in the EU holding a mandate from a third-country provider.
- **Importer (Article 3(6)):** first places an AI system carrying a third-country trademark on the EU market.
- **Distributor (Article 3(7)):** every other actor in the supply chain, other than the provider and the importer.

**Change of role (Article 25):** whoever substantially modifies an AI system becomes the provider, with the full set of obligations. Most German SMEs start as deployers. Not all of them stay there.
sections.keyTakeaway: Article 3(3) to (7) defines four roles: provider, deployer, importer, distributor. Most SMEs are deployers.

sections.title: Where the role flips
sections.content:
**Case 1 (deployer):** A machinery builder buys a predictive-maintenance model from a startup and fits it into his own plant. He uses the system, he does not retrain it. Role: deployer.

**Case 2 (provider):** The same machinery builder trains the model further on his own sensor data and sells the plant, model included, under his own trademark. Further training is a substantial modification (Article 3(23)). The role flips: provider, with the full conformity-assessment duty where the system is high-risk (Article 25).

**Case 3 (deployer):** The HR lead uses Personio with AI matching switched on to shortlist applicants. Personio is the provider. The employer is the deployer, with obligations of its own, because applicant matching is a high-risk use case (Annex III, point 4).

**Case 4 (importer):** An HR consultant sells a US applicant-screening bot through her website to German clients. The US provider has no EU establishment, so she is the importer.

What does that mean for you? White-label an AI system, change it substantially, or sell it under your own trademark, and you are the provider. With everything that comes with it (Article 25).
sections.keyTakeaway: Further training, or selling under your own trademark, turns a deployer into a provider (Article 3(23), Article 25). The compliance work grows sharply.

sections.title: Operator or not: the private exemption (Article 2(10))
sections.content:
Article 3(8) gathers all four roles, plus authorised representatives and product manufacturers, under one term: **operator**. Once you are an operator, Article 4 on AI literacy applies at a minimum, whatever your precise role.

So whoever uses or sells AI professionally is caught. The open question is only which set of obligations applies.

**The private exemption (Article 2(10))**

A person who uses AI **exclusively in a personal, non-professional activity**, ChatGPT for her own texts, images, or tax return, is **not a deployer within the meaning of the Regulation**. Article 2(10) expressly carves out purely private use by natural persons. Concretely:

- A private individual planning a holiday with ChatGPT: **not caught**.
- The same person as an employee, writing customer correspondence with ChatGPT for her employer: **caught**, because the employer uses it professionally as a deployer under Article 3(4).
- A managing director drafting quotations with ChatGPT: **caught**, because her company counts as deployer.

The AI Act governs professional use and placing on the market. What you do at home for yourself is none of its business.
sections.keyTakeaway: Whoever uses AI exclusively in private is not a deployer within the meaning of the Regulation: Article 2(10) carves purely private use out. Professional use is caught, however small the business.

quiz.questionText: A machinery manufacturer buys a predictive-maintenance model, further trains it on its own sensor data, and sells the machine including the model under its own trademark. What role does it have?

answerOptions.text: Deployer, because it uses the model itself
Provider, because it substantially modifies the model and places it on the market under its own trademark
Distributor, because it only resells the model
Importer, because the model originally came from a startup

quiz.explanation: Article 3(3) defines a provider by reference to placing a system on the market under its own name or trademark. Further training can constitute a substantial modification under Article 3(23), triggering the change to the provider role under Article 25.

quiz.questionText: Who is NOT within the scope of the AI Act?

answerOptions.text: A managing director who uses ChatGPT to draft quotations
A private individual who uses ChatGPT at home to prepare a tax return
An SME using Personio with AI applicant matching enabled
A freelancer who uses Copilot for client presentations

quiz.explanation: Article 2(10) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 excludes natural persons who use AI systems in the course of a purely personal, non-professional activity. Once the use forms part of a professional activity, the Regulation applies (Article 3(4)).

quiz.questionText: What role does an SME have when it uses an AI system supplied by a US provider for its own operations without modifying it?

answerOptions.text: Deployer
Importer
Provider
Distributor

quiz.explanation: Article 3(4) defines the deployer as the person using an AI system under its authority. An importer under Article 3(6) is the person that first places the third-country system on the EU market, not a person that merely uses it.

lessons.title: Extraterritorial scope
lessons.subtitle: Why your US SaaS provider falls under the AI Act the moment its output is used in Germany.

sections.title: The output trigger: Article 2(1), point (c)
sections.content:
OpenAI in San Francisco produces a contract summary. A clerk in Nuremberg reads it. That alone brings OpenAI inside the scope of the AI Act.

The rule behind it: Article 2(1), point (c), of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 covers providers and deployers of AI systems established in a third country where the output produced by the system is used in the Union. What counts is where the output lands.

**Consequence:** a US provider placing an AI system on the EU market has to appoint an authorised representative in the EU wherever Article 22 requires one. Without that appointment it may not place the system on the market at all.

Recital 22 gives the reason. The output trigger is there to prevent circumvention of the Regulation and to secure effective protection for natural persons located in the Union. Without the clause, providers would have moved their servers to Nevada and carried on.

**For you:** the provider's obligations stay with the US provider. Ask in the vendor conversation how it meets them, and ask before you sign.
sections.keyTakeaway: Article 2(1), point (c), makes the AI Act extraterritorial. Once the output is used in the EU, the Regulation applies to third-country providers too. Recital 22 gives the reason: circumvention.

sections.title: The authorised representative, the required EU contact point
sections.content:
Article 3(5) defines the **authorised representative** as a natural or legal person located or established in the EU holding a written mandate to perform a provider's obligations. Article 22 turns that into a duty for third-country providers of high-risk AI systems covered by the provision. The representative performs the tasks set out in the mandate on the provider's behalf.

OpenAI in Ireland, Microsoft in Ireland, Salesforce, Workday. All of them run EU entities or representation arrangements, and Article 22 is one legal reason why.

Three questions belong in the next vendor contract.

- **Who is the EU authorised representative?** Article 22: name, registered office, contact details.
- **Does the technical documentation under Article 11 exist?** If it does, have access on request written into the contract.
- **How has the system been classified?** Prohibited practice, high risk under Annex III or Annex I, an Article 50 transparency case, minimal risk, or a general-purpose AI model?

A vendor who cannot answer these quickly cannot substantiate its AI Act compliance.
sections.keyTakeaway: Third-country providers of high-risk AI systems covered by Article 22 need an EU authorised representative (Article 3(5), Article 22). Have that contact named in the vendor contract.

sections.title: Brussels Effect 2.0 for German SMEs
sections.content:
When your SaaS provider has to implement the AI Act, part of the work arrives finished. Provider-side transparency under Article 50, technical documentation, any conformity assessment that applies: the provider does that for its own system. The groundwork helps every customer. It does not replace your own deployer obligations.

But your deployer obligations stay with you. Article 26 lists them for high-risk AI systems. Follow the provider's instructions for use, ensure human oversight, keep the logs where required, check that input data under your control is relevant and sufficiently representative. And Article 4 on AI literacy binds every operator, you included.

Two levels that interlock. Neither replaces the other.

Concretely: write provider-compliance clauses into every new SaaS contract. Have the applicable declaration of conformity and the authorised representative confirmed in writing. A vendor that dodges is not ready. And at the end of it, you answer for your own deployer obligations.
sections.keyTakeaway: The Brussels Effect can deliver US systems with the provider-side work already done. Articles 26 and 4 stay with you: vendor compliance is not deployer compliance.

quiz.questionText: A US SaaS provider has no establishment in the EU. Its AI output is used by an SME in Bavaria. Does the AI Act apply to the provider?

answerOptions.text: Yes, because of the output-in-the-EU trigger in Article 2(1), point (c)
No, because it is established outside the EU
Only if it actively markets the system in the EU
Only if its servers are located in the EU

quiz.explanation: Article 2(1), point (c), of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 covers third-country providers where the output produced by the system is used in the EU. Recital 22 confirms that this is a deliberate anti-circumvention rule.

quiz.questionText: What is the role of an authorised representative under Article 3(5)?

answerOptions.text: The representative replaces all obligations of the third-country provider
The representative is established in the EU and performs AI Act tasks on behalf of the provider under a written mandate
The representative must be a German lawyer
The representative is required only for general-purpose AI models

quiz.explanation: Article 3(5) defines an authorised representative as a person located or established in the EU with a written mandate. Article 22 requires covered third-country providers of high-risk AI systems to appoint one. The representative acts for the provider but does not replace it.

quiz.questionText: What should an SME ask a US AI provider during vendor assessment?

answerOptions.text: Only the price; every other matter belongs to the vendor
Its authorised representative, technical documentation, and risk classification
Only its GDPR privacy notice
Only the country where its servers are located

quiz.explanation: Article 26 creates deployer obligations that cannot be met without relevant provider information. You need to know the EU authorised representative under Article 22, whether Article 11 technical documentation exists, and how the system has been classified.

lessons.title: Timeline: February 2025, August 2025, August 2026, December 2027, August 2028
lessons.subtitle: Phased application. AI literacy and the prohibitions already apply, Article 50 follows in August 2026, and the high-risk dates for 2027 and 2028 have been law since July 2026.

sections.title: The application dates and the amended high-risk timetable
sections.content:
Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 entered into force on **1 August 2024**. Nothing applied all at once. It arrives in stages:

- **2 February 2025:** Article 4 on AI literacy and most of the prohibitions in Article 5 apply.
- **2 August 2025:** the rules for general-purpose AI models, the governance structure, and much of the penalties framework become applicable; Commission enforcement against providers of general-purpose AI models starts on **2 August 2026**.
- **27 July 2026:** Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 enters into force and amends Article 4, individual prohibitions, transitional provisions, and the high-risk timetable, among other things.
- **2 August 2026:** the transparency obligations in Article 50 and further general application points bite.
- **2 December 2027:** high-risk rules for stand-alone systems under Article 6(2) and Annex III.
- **2 August 2028:** high-risk rules for product-embedded systems under Article 6(1) and Annex I.

The high-risk dates are applicable law under the published amending regulation. Systems that reached the market before the new dates have transitional rules of their own.
sections.keyTakeaway: Article 4 has applied since February 2025 and was amended with effect from 27 July 2026. Article 50 bites from 2 August 2026. The high-risk dates of 2 December 2027 and 2 August 2028 are applicable law.

sections.title: Your tasks per deadline
sections.content:
**Position as of 28 July 2026:** Article 4 prescribes no particular form of documentation, and since the amendment it no longer asks operators to guarantee an individual level of competence. What it does ask of providers and deployers are measures that support the development of AI literacy in a way that fits the context.

**Now:**

- a complete inventory of every AI system in the house, shadow IT included
- a risk classification per system, against Annex III, Article 5, the general-purpose AI rules, or the low-risk remainder
- documented Article 4 measures that fit the role and the risk
- the transparency and interaction notices under Article 50 in place by 2 August 2026, wherever the conditions are met

**For 2027 and 2028:**

- plan stand-alone high-risk obligations for **2 December 2027**
- plan product-embedded high-risk systems for **2 August 2028**
- prepare vendor documents, logs, human oversight, and any fundamental rights impact assessment that may be required

**Grandfathering has a catch.** A substantial modification can end transitional treatment or trigger a fresh assessment. So every major update means: classify again.
sections.keyTakeaway: The AI inventory, context-appropriate Article 4 measures, and Article 50 preparation are the work in front of you now. The high-risk dates in 2027 and 2028 are applicable law.

sections.title: When does enforcement begin?
sections.content:
Article 99 of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 tiers the fines in three levels. For undertakings, the higher of the two figures usually applies:

- **Prohibited practices under Article 5:** up to **EUR 35 million or 7%** of total worldwide annual turnover (Article 99(3)).
- **The obligations listed in Article 99(4):** up to **EUR 15 million or 3%**.
- **Incorrect information supplied to authorities:** up to **EUR 7.5 million or 1%** (Article 99(5)).

**SME clause:** SMEs, and since the amendment small mid-caps too, have upper limits of their own. The calculation, and which penalty provision an infringement belongs to, need a look at the individual case.

Article 4 has applied since 2 February 2025, in the form amended by Regulation (EU) 2026/1744. National supervision and enforcement begin in early August 2026, according to the Commission FAQ. Article 50 becomes applicable on 2 August 2026. Whether a fine is on the table depends on the provision infringed, its application date, the competent authority, and the case itself.

The high-risk dates, 2 December 2027 for stand-alone Annex III systems and 2 August 2028 for product-embedded Annex I systems, have been law since 27 July 2026.
sections.keyTakeaway: Article 4 has applied since February 2025, in the form amended on 27 July 2026. National supervision and enforcement begin in early August 2026, according to the Commission FAQ.

quiz.questionText: From which date has the obligation to support sufficient AI literacy under Article 4 applied?

answerOptions.text: 2 August 2026
2 February 2025
2 August 2027
1 August 2024

quiz.explanation: Article 113, point (a), of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689: Chapter I, which contains Article 4, and Chapter II apply from 2 February 2025. The duty has been in force since that date. The Commission FAQ names 2 August 2026 as the start of national supervision and enforcement.

quiz.questionText: Which date did Parliament and the Council adopt for stand-alone high-risk systems under Annex III?

answerOptions.text: 2 August 2025
2 August 2026
2 August 2027
2 December 2027

quiz.explanation: Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, which entered into force on 27 July 2026, specifies 2 December 2027 for stand-alone high-risk systems under Annex III and 2 August 2028 for high-risk systems embedded in products under Annex I.

quiz.questionText: What is the maximum fine for an infringement of the prohibitions in Article 5?

answerOptions.text: EUR 7.5 million or 1% of turnover
EUR 15 million or 3% of turnover
EUR 35 million or 7% of turnover, whichever is higher
EUR 50 million or 10% of turnover

quiz.explanation: Article 99(3) provides for administrative fines of up to EUR 35 million or 7% of total worldwide annual turnover for infringements of the prohibited practices listed in Article 5. For SMEs, Article 99(6) caps the fine at the lower of the two amounts.
